messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Student
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 78

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed, Authority Presence: Police, Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Avoid Eye Contact: Making eye contact with other people, Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons
  Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kiet had been twenty when he deployed to the northern provinces of a fractured country, riding in a white relief convoy tasked with delivering medical supplies to isolated clinics. On the third week, their route crossed a narrow bridge checkpoint manned by armed men in mismatched fatigues. The guards ordered them out of the vehicles, rifles held loose but ready, while Kiet was made to stand under a harsh floodlight, feeling the weight of dozens of eyes tracking his every movement. He spent those hours trying to negotiate passage for a group of displaced families waiting at the end of the road, his voice rising over the tension until his throat gave out. When the situation escalated and the families were turned away, he carried the quiet certainty that his presence had changed nothing. He returned to the United States after his contract ended, holding firmly to the belief that he had failed in his most important role as a relief worker. Back in his home state, Kiet enrolled in a community college to study public health. The campus quickly became a landscape of unspoken threats. He was certain that any security guard walking the quad in a crisp uniform carried the same silent weight he had felt under the checkpoint floodlight, so he began cutting through side alleys to avoid the main administrative building. When a local law enforcement officer directed traffic near his apartment complex, his pulse spiked and his breath caught, the old sensation of being watched closing in. He stopped answering calls from his college friends, avoiding the quiet of his dorm where the faces of people he had socialised with before the war zone would replay in his mind. In conversation, he trained himself never to meet anyone’s eyes, keeping his gaze fixed on the floor or the back of his laptop. Over the months, these choices calcified into habits. He missed a group project deadline because he could not walk past the campus security office without his hands shaking, and he stopped attending a volunteer orientation at a local shelter after seeing an officer escorting a donor vehicle. His body had become a traitor; even sitting in his quiet dorm room, his muscles tightened and his stomach knotted as if he were still standing under that unforgiving light. He had come to believe that his body kept reacting as if he were still in danger, even when he was perfectly safe, and that made resting feel impossible. It was the accumulation of these parallel strains that finally brought Kiet to the university counseling center last Tuesday. He had sat through two full lectures while the campus police conducted a routine training exercise in the courtyard below, forcing himself to remain in his seat as long as he could before the uniform and the radio static pushed him to his feet. He knew he could no longer navigate his classes or his daily routine without constant exhaustion dragging at his shoulders. What frightened him most was the certainty that he would never be able to stop bad things from happening, that every interaction carried the risk of another collapse. He had hoped that stepping into the clinic might at least quiet the relentless scanning of the room and help him remember how to exist in a world that no longer required him to carry the weight of other people’s survival. He was ready to try, as long as it meant he could finally put down the armor he had been wearing for months.
